_comment: Throughput baseline for bench/regression-gate.sh, and the committed record
every figure on docs/benchmarks.md resolves to. Raising this is a
deliberate act in a commit, the same as the documentation ratchets in
tests/docs_drift_test.rs. Do NOT lower it to make a red run pass: that
records a regression as the new normal, which is precisely how the 0.5.84
drop survived four releases.
The figure is 4-core offline reconstruction over the fixed-state 535k
corpus that bench/carrier.py generates (5000 calls, 100 Call-IDs, 200
streams). Four cores is both the peak of the curve and its most
reproducible point.
Measured on a LOCAL release build of the recorded commit, not on a release
artifact -- the gate has to catch a regression the day it lands, not once
it has shipped.
WHAT THE PUBLISHED FIGURE IS. The LOWEST of the three replicates, for
every core count, on the page as well as here. Publishing the lowest is
what makes the two numbers the same number: a floor derived from it cannot
sit above a figure this host actually produces, and a reader who re-runs
the harness meets or beats the published value rather than falling short
of a median. Before 2026-09-09 the page and this file each picked their own
figure, and that is how they came apart the third time -- the page
headlined 3.23M for 0.5.122 while this file recorded 3.25M with replicates
3.25/3.29/3.29M, so the published number was one the recorded run never
produced.
WHY THE RAISES HAVE BEEN LARGE, AND WHAT IT COST TO LEARN. An entry once
recorded 0.5.104's 2.28M and was never raised when 0.5.108 lifted the real
figure by mapping the capture file. docs/benchmarks.md was updated that
day; this file was not. So when 0.5.118 introduced a defect that cost 27%
-- is_merged read the ENTIRE capture into memory before rejecting it on
the first four bytes -- the tool fell to 2.40M, which is 105% of a
baseline recorded four releases earlier. The gate passed. It passed on
every release from 0.5.118 to 0.5.121 while the shipped binary was a
quarter slower than the page advertising it.
That is this file's own warning, come true a second time, and it is left
in the paragraph below because it was already written down and still did
not prevent this. The lesson is narrower than 'keep it fresh': a raise in
docs/benchmarks.md and a raise here are the SAME event, and doing one
without the other converts a 20% gate into a 31% one silently. Whoever
re-measures that page re-measures this file in the same commit.
AND THAT SENTENCE IS NOW ENFORCED RATHER THAN ASKED FOR. It was a
convention written in a comment for three separations running.
benchmarks_pages_headline_matches_the_committed_baseline in
tests/site_journey_test.rs binds this file to BOTH hand-maintained copies
of the benchmarks page and to the homepage tile, so moving any one of them
alone is a red test rather than a discovery six releases later.

measured._version: main after the v0.5.211 tag, which reports 0.5.211: the tag plus the single-core reader change (#451).
measured.host: NVIDIA Jetson Thor devboard (aarch64), 14 cores, PREEMPT_RT, idle
measured.method: median-of-5 after one discarded warmup, three replicates
measured.idle_gate: vmstat id >= 96% and no toolchain build process; 90% would permit 1.4 busy cores on a 14-core host
measured._peak_rss_published: The page's peak RSS cell is the HIGHEST of the three replicates, the figure to plan memory against.
measured._session: vmstat idle 99% before every run; no runner job, rustc or cargo process.
measured._note: Baseline and every published figure are the LOWEST replicate, not the median, so the floor derived from them cannot sit above a figure this host actually produces.
measured._eight_cores: Eight cores is SLOWER than four on this host and this corpus, in all three replicates. That is the shape of the curve here, not a bad run, and the page says so rather than quoting the peak and leaving the shoulder off.

_comment: The other table on docs/benchmarks.md, recorded here for the same reason:
a figure with no committed record is a figure nobody can check. Growing
state rather than fixed state -- unique Call-IDs and unique RTP endpoints
per call (--call-ids 0 --stream-pairs 0), measured at --cores 4.
One measurement each, median-of-5 after a discarded warmup, from the same
session and host as the multi-core table above.
carrier_scale_sweep._session_spread: Two more sessions the same evening measured this build at 3.14-3.31M at 20,000 calls: the sweep moves about 8% between sessions, more than within one. In an interleaved session, 0.5.160, 0.5.211 and this build were within 5% of each other at every size: 0.5.160 was fastest at 500 calls and slowest at 20,000.

_floor_rationale: The regression this gate exists to catch was 40%. Run-to-run spread is ~2%
on an idle host and ~10% when something else shares it, so 20% sits clear
of both. A tighter band on a runner that also serves CI would be flaky in
the direction that gets a gate muted, and a muted gate catches nothing.
The floor is 2.82M. Checked against the numbers that matter here: the
0.5.118 regression measured 2.40M, which is 68% and trips it -- the whole
point of keeping the baseline current. 0.5.122's 3.25M is 92% and does
not, which is correct: 0.5.122 was not a regression, it was an older tool.
Note what the raise fixed, three times now. While this file baselined
0.5.89's 1.89M, the floor sat at 1.51M against a tool running at 2.28M --
a 34% drop would have passed a gate whose stated band is 20%. While it
baselined 0.5.104's 2.28M, a tool running at 3.30M could lose 27% and
pass. While it baselined 0.5.122's 3.25M, a tool running at 3.56M could
lose 27% and pass. A stale baseline does not merely under-report; it
silently widens the band it advertises.
The 2026-10-11 re-measure moved the baseline DOWN, from 3.56M to 3.52M,
and that is not the move the warning above forbids. Nothing was red: it
is the lowest replicate of a full re-measure (3.56 / 3.56 / 3.52M), 1.1%
under the old figure and inside the ~2% noise floor, and the same session
measured 0.5.211 at 3.43 / 3.53 / 3.56M. Publishing the lowest replicate
is the rule this file states; keeping 3.56M would publish a figure this
run did not produce at its floor.
